I would be one of the first to recognize the fact that the recipients of
the Psi U Diamond are the luckiest people in the world. They were
lucky to be selected out of a numerous student body to be pledged to
some chapter of our Fraternity. They were lucky to have grown into
young manhood in the association of others who had been chosen as
potential, and ultimate, members earlier, and who, in their turn were
the beneficiaries of the workings of that nebulous thing called "Luck."
As out in life each of the readers has wended his way, he carried
with him the memories, the joys and the unsung contributions that his
life in his chapter gave to each�the discipline that makes living with
those around him far simpler and ever so much more tolerable. The
give and take of chapter life serves him well every day of his life.
That same discipline often gives him the edge that outsiders do not
have and must yet acquire if they are to keep up with the "Chosen
Few."
No matter how old or how young, all to whom the postman brings
The Diamond cannot but help being reminded of the undeniable fact
that once one became a Psi U one is forever a Psi U. Any doubt about
that should be dispeUed when The Diamond arrives via Uncle Sam's
Pony Express. This should also bring to mind that Psi Upsilon is a tre
mendous entity of which each of us is an integral part. Also, that no
entity, great or small, can long exist if the parts fall away from the main
structure.
This all boils down to one thing. Rich or poor, young or old, fat or
slim, in the best of health or otherwise, each one is a part of a truly
great Fraternity. Those few Brothers who are selected to guide the
destinies of Psi Upsilon want you to know that each one of us is an
mtegral part of something that is more than worthwhile. They want
you to share with equal pride the accomphshments of the organization.
They also want you, in accordance with your ability, to do what you
can to make the burden easier at the top. You may support your chap
ter. You may recruit the interest of young men about to attend a col
lege or university where there is a chapter of Psi Upsilon. And you
can pay the only truly voluntary dues I know of if it is within your
ability to do so.
Nobody asked me, but the temptation could not be resisted to try
to epitomize what all of us think but, alas and alack, too many of us
leave off right there.

The Governor
Will Run!
Brother Nelson A.
Rockefeller, Zeta '30
Announces Candi
dacy for Presidency
of United States.
No presidential candidate ever got a
campaign
off to a faster start than did Brother Nelson A.
Rockefeller on Tuesday, April 30. About 11:00
that morning the Governor announced his decision
to run for the nomination for the Presidency of the
United States on the Repubhcan ticket. By 8:00
that evening, when the polls closed, he had won
all of the convention delegates from the state of
Massachusetts�end he had not even been on the
ballot!
Brother Rockefeller's announcement came after
some earlier false starts, one of which was a com
pletely surprising annoimcement that he would not
run unless he was drafted by party leaders. Now
he apparently feels that the insistence of certain
Republican Party leaders has been strong enough
to warrant his joining the fray.
The New York governor's entrance into the race
adds further interest to an aheady comphcated
race for the nominations. The crusading Senator
McCarthy has captured the hearts of many of the
youthful voters, and his showing in the primary
races has been almost miraculous. The political
acumen and calculation of Robert Kennedy wiU
stand him in good stead throughout the fight,
though he has yet to run as well as McCarthy. The
man who is apparently "anointed" is Mr. Hum
phrey, though the President is being very careful

3
not to commit himself to any candidate at this
time.
On the Republican side of the fence Brother
Rockefeller faces a Richard M. Nixon who is an
entirely different figure from the man who faced
John F. Kennedy in 1960. He is a warmer man
with ideas of great dynamism. The press has found
him charming and sensible, and his recent state
ment dealing with the "urban problem," as re
ported on p. 21 of Time Magazine for May 3, 1968,
is an understanding and human evaluation of a
very diflBcult situation.
Brother Rockefeller is a man more given to
promises than Mr. Nixon, and many of his ideas are
more expansive. What the Rockefeller of today is
politically can be seen in remarkably fine germ in
a monograph entitled The Future of Federalism,
pubhshed during the 30's. He has a very definite
philosophy of balance between the functions of
private enterprise and government.
In relation to the other candidate, however.
Brother Rockefeller's most outstanding advantage
lies in his long experience as an executive. He has
served as Undersecretary of State for Latin Ameri
can Affairs, and has been governor of the State of
New York for nine years. There can be little argu
ment that the position of President of the United
States is a
position demanding executive acumen.
In the race itseff, however, there are men who
have the ability to handle the office. What sets the
fight for the nominations off from those of the past,
however, is the meticulous and important atten
tion that has been given to the issues at stake. This
is no battle over personalities : it is a fight over who
will lead the nation with what ideas and policies.
Not since the depression has a campaign con
cerned itself so thoroughly with the issues�nor
has one needed to. The urban problem is becom
ing increasingly difficult to handle, the war in
Vietnam is a bone of contention, and the dollar is
in grave danger at the hands of overseas nations
and speculators (not to mention the economic
havoc wreaked by inflation in our own country).
To these questions each of the candidates has
turned his attention, and each one has ideas which
are different from the next. Into this melange
Brother Rockefeller has walked, and while we are
not a political publication we offer our wishes to
Brother Rockefeller for good luck in the months
ahead.

The Headmaster's
Answer Was NO
by John C. Esty, Jr., Gamma '50
The following article was a speech delivered to
the parents and alumni of the Taft School by head
master Esty at a planning conference held last
October.
Prior to going to Taft Brother Esty served as
the Freshman Dean at his alma mater Amherst.
Last May a boy came to me with an unusual
request. He was planning a summer job in the
woods, where he thought it would be appropriate
for him to grow a beard. His request was that he
be allowed to return in the fall and have the beard
at Taft. I pointed out that this would obviously
make some problems, and I wondered why he
wanted to have a beard. He said he wasn't rebel
ling or protesting anything; he just thought he
might look better. I said I'd think it over and let
him know in a few days. I then mentioned the
question to a number of my colleagues, and we
agreed that�
for a variety of reasons �
Taft wasn't
quite ready for beards. When the boy came back
for his answer, I told him that I didn't think it
would work, but that I'd like to see him with his
beard. He was to come to see me on opening day
and I would make the final decision then. 1
thanked him for being thoughtful enough to dis
cuss it with me. 1 also told him that the decision
would most probably be negative.
During the summer I thought about the problem
on and off, with considerable concern. I was quite
sure we really couldn't allow the beard, but I
wasn't sure just why or whether that was
right. It
seemed to depend finally on our basic objectives
at Taft: If we are mostly concerned with ap
pearances, then the beard comes off; but if we are
truly concerned about individual growth then
maybe the beard could mean
something vaguely
important to this boy. Clearly the right course lay
somewhere in between, but I settled it temporari
ly by convincing myself that his beard, at that
very moment, was probably starting to itch. It
would never get under way and there would be
no problem.
On opening day the boy walked into my office
with a rich, full beard, neatly trimmed and looking
astonishingly impressive. He was there for the
decision. 1 asked him what he thought I was going
to say. Without hostility, he said he thought the
answer would be no. I replied that he was correct,
but because the beard obviously meant something
to him, and because he had discussed it with me
earlier, 1 wanted him to know why. I explained
that I felt hair length, beards, and dress in gener
al were morally neutral; that I thought, in fact,
he looked quite well with his beard; and that I
wished we had the kind of society where people
did not become preoccupied with such things. I
felt, however, that a beard these days could, un
fortunately, be symbolic of too many things that I
did not want Taft to stand for: flabby shortcuts to
self-awareness, passive protest rather than active
conviction, over-indulgent self-pity, and excessive
concentration on the superficial trappings of indi
vidualism.
I think he understood what I was trying to say;
at least I hope he did. He was obviously disap
pointed, but he stood up, thanked me for con
sidering his request�and went off and shaved his
beard.
1 mention this episode at some
length ( and pos
sibly it will seem too drawn out for what, after all,
should be a simple matter), because it illustrates
two important aspects in the lives of young people
today. It shows, first, the enormous complexity
of young lives, which develop with so many op
tions and choices formerly constrained by arbi
trarily drawn strictures. But more importantly, I
mean it to illustrate what I think is the only real
answer to the resultant confusion and tensions.

In the absence of the old ground rules, mutual
trust and continuing relationship are more vital
than ever!
It seems to me that the common denominator
in all the disturbing eruptions of youthful dis
content of the past three years is the absence of
trust, the failure of relationship. I consider this
"generational gap" to be the greatest psychologi
cal problem in the country today. One sees ex
amples on every hand. A recent article in the
Harvard Alumni Magazine points out how the use
of marijuana may be seen in this light. The point
is not that marijuana is just like alcohol in its
use and effect�whether more or less detrimental to
health�but that it is different! It is unknown, mys
terious, unfamiliar to an older generation, and,
therefore, uniquely a special possession of the
younger.
So what is oiu- response? What is our respon
sibility as parents or as teachers? For one thing,
we cannot simply throw up our hands and say
we don't understand. Otherwise, we are in the
position of a
plumber who goes out on a job and
has to confess that he doesn't understand much
about pipes. There are plenty of good books and
articles available on the present phenomena, and
I think we have an
obligation to be familiar with
them. (The Faculty is being asked to read at least
Youth and the Hazards of Affluence, by Graham
B. Blaine, Jr., M.D., Harper and Row, 1966. )
But we can't stop with just understanding; a
more active quest and purpose is necessary. We
do indeed need standards and guidelines, and they
need to be firmly imposed�
but they should flow
from understanding and take meaning within rela
tionship! We must understand that the youthful
bid for freedom of choice or a "leave me alone"
philosophy is almost always accompanied, at a
deeper level, by the need for guidance and sup
port. I would almost formulate something like an
inverse law: the more a young person seeks to
make himself unattractive by bizarre dress or be
havior, the more he actually needs wise and
sympathetic counsel in setting goals and pulling
himseff together. The problem is that by the time
these outward signs are visible, the inner resistance
is almost insuperable; it may then be too late. But
that is not to deny the need. I think of the boy at
Taft who impressed us all by his prickly indepen
dence, his immunity to guidance, his aloof individuahsm. He loved to run cross-country, before
5
it became an
organized sport at Taft. One day
he telegraphed his real feelings in part of a poem
he wrote for his Enghsh teacher:
It is late.
It is late and
I'm still running. I am a
Running partner with Confusion
And have no direction.
It is late and
The icy, northwest wind
Clamps his chilly teeth
Onto my tired Spirit;
I am uncertain whether
To accept his attack or.
To struggle within myself for
The courage to continue.
Life must guide me in my Chaos.
Someone must guide me;
Please, someone.
That leads me to the role I think Taft can
play
in these times of confusion in the lives of young
people. Let me state this as a series of propositions.
�
Young people ai-e the life blood of a society or
nation.
� There must be a process by which young people
are brought into the historical mainstream of a
society or nation�a process which is true to that
history and its traditions, yet which can recognize
the need for change and nurture openness to
change.
� This process�which we call education�com
prises both substance and method, both history
and technique, both new knowledge and old. But
its most precious component is what we might call
humane arts�how people express beauty, aspira
tion, the meaning of life, and sensibility to other
people, other Societies and other Nations.
� The substance of the humane arts is less im
portant than the context within which they are
taught or conveyed. This kind of education, al
most by definition, must involve personal relation
ship, emotion, feeling, humor, anger, sadness�but
in any case the personal contact of one human
being with another.
The task of a fraternity and its leadership is very
similar to this, isn't it?�Ed.

Individuality and Fraternity
In the November, 1951, issue of the Atlantic
Monthly Brother Archibald MacLeish, Beta '15,
had an article entitled "To Make Men Free." On
page 27 of that issue he said ". . . the American
citadel is a man. Not man in general. Not man in
the abstract. Not the majority of men. But man.
That man. His worth. His uniqueness." He also
speaks of freedom in terms of "freedom of the indi
vidual human being to think for himself and to
come to the truth by the light of his own mind and
conscience . . .
[not] freedom to be like everybody
else." These are thoughts which stand well by
themselves in the ideals of American History.
We hear much talk today about civil rights; and
the ideal of civil rights seems much abused when
many criminals must be allowed to go free be
cause of technicalities in the law which protect
their "civil rights." Even so MacLeish's very
American sentiments are behind the legal tech
nicalities which protect the rights of Americans,
whether or not they are criminals. The many indi
cations of social turmoil in this country today are
endemic to a society that is becoming "individual
oriented" in its great haste to avoid being simply
"mass oriented."
Suddenly in the context of such turmoil the
meaning of fraternity can assume a new and vital
role. Fraternities have always been seen as "la
boratories of democracy." Today they are
being
questioned in many ways. Many educational insti
tutions see them as
nothing more than extra, muchneeded housing. In too many places they are
regarded as inherently "anti-inteUectual," and as
hotbeds of innumerable vices, real and imagined.
Perhaps because of their selectivity, fraternities are
undemocratic? It is unfortunate that the meaning
of the word Democracy has become so clouded
today that it is a bad word for communication. It
is very nearly useless to argue this particular point.
Perhaps for today a fraternity's greatest value
hes in the fact that it can be (and many are) a
place where the individual can learn that he is
important as an individual only as
long as he
has a contribution to make toward common
goals.
The individual can discover here that he is use
less, both to himself and to the fratemity, when he
cannot put himself in some way into the progress
of the corporate body�the "brotherhood." This is
not to say, of course, that conformity should be a
fact of life in a fraternity. This is, indeed, not the
case. Too much conformity can be as
stifling to
worthwhile goal accomplishment as too many
iminterested individuals.
In short, freedom for the individual is meaning
less unless it exists in a social context. The fratemi
ty provides a social context small enough to be
useful, and large enough to be effective in awaken
ing social consciousness and responsible freedom
in the individual.

New York, N.Y. 10036 USA
Dear Brothers:
My copy of The Diamond (Winter 1968) has
just reached me here. It is full of good things, a
very interesting issue. There are several reminders
that communications of various kinds are
request
ed from readers. Taking you at your word, here
are some rambling thoughts from an octogenarian
presently in foreign lands. If they do not meet
your requirements for publication�Hell, every
editor has a wastebasket. Use it.
In my college years (1901-1905) spent in the
Halls of the Delta, Psi Upsilon was so pre-eminent
in all institutions where we had chapters that our
grand fraternity was truly in a class by itself. This
status remained during the years when, as an
alumnus, I took an active part in the Delta Cor
poration. In my blissful ignorance, I thought the
supremacy to be everlasting.
Verily, pride goeth before a fall. It seems we
became a crowd of complacent fat cats who
thought that like the lilies of the field we could

live in glory without toiling or
spinning. The rude
awakening was a
very bitter blow to our pride.
It takes years to reach a
pinnacle, only a brief time
to slip backwards.
Having left the East in 1940 to reside in Cali
fornia, 1 got out of touch with the Delta and
Psi U. affairs in general. It was not until the late
1950's that I became aware of our
retrogression.
A grand nephew of mine was about
to enter Brown. His father is not a .
college man but his grandfather, my
brother John W. DuB. Gould was
Delta 1902. This seemed a natural
legacy, so I wrote to the Sigma where
I had several friends among the alum
ni. The chapter was
ready to pledge
the young man. To my surprise, he
said Psi U. was not for him. He felt that life at the
chapter house would not be conducive to attain
ing the education he desired. He joined no fra
ternity, made Phi Beta Kappa and was graduated
cum laude. What an asset was lost to our brothers
at Brown and how proud I would have been to
have him wear the Diamond badge!
Please forgive this personal episode. It is men
tioned to show how old timers are shaken by the
unexpected misfortunes of our beloved Psi U.
Fortunately, we are not a bunch of sissies. We
shall fight our way back to the top. While it is
humiliating to learn that a number of fraternities
we used to consider second grade are now rated
above us, there is a
great consolation. None of
them will ever reach the heights we once
gained,
and D.V. will regain, because none has our heri
tage. Our founders had an idealism and a
concep
tion of true brotherhood that is unique in the
annals of American fraternities. Thank God, they
passed this on to us.
So instead of crying in our beer, we did some
thing about it. Such stalwart warriors as Robert
Parsons, Alfred Morton,
Jerome Brush and many
I other toilers in the vine-
! yard have led the way.
With such inspired lead
ership, those of us in the
back benches had to fol
low. But did we? There
are indications that a num
ber of us answered the call of duty, but not
enough. With so much at stake, all Psi' U's should
lay it on the line�money, encouragement and faith
in our destiny. Like MacArthur, "We shall return!"
My small contribution is given cheerfully for I
feel the Diamond of Upsilon is a priceless jewel
that must be preserved, no matter what the cost.
On the way to Switzerland in 1967, it was
my
good fortune to attend the annual Delta Dinner
at the Lotus Club in New York. Frank Booth,
Frank Russell, Joe Esquirol, Russ McShane, Ted
Richards and other old friends were there and
gave me a
hearty welcome, as did members of
the active chapter. All told, as pleasant a crew
of buccaneers as ever scuttled a
ship or got an
elder brother soused.
Now a word to you Editors, I am one myself.
Enclosed is a
copy of "Bottles and Bins," a
quar
terly that will be sent gratis upon request to
Charles Krug Winery, St. Helena, California
94574. You are
doing a fine job. The Diamond
is more readable than ever before. It has become
a vital factor in the renaissance of Psi Upsilon.
Asking for communications is a good slant. It has
the twofold result of broadening the news cover
age and making others do your work, something
no editor should overlook. Keep up the good
work.
Yours in the Bonds,
Francis Lewis Gould
Delta 1905

DELTA INITIATES
SIXTEEN
by Joseph A. Esquirol, Delta '17
Perhaps the best indication of the solid orienta
tion of a
group of pledges by a dedicated pledgemaster was demonstrated on February 26 last
when 16 candidates for membership in the Delta
Chapter exchanged their novitiate status for proud
wearers of the Badge of Psi Upsilon. Together
these 16 (the second largest group of pledges to
be initiated into the mysteries of Psi Upsilon at
the Delta Chapter) stood up to their assignments
and after a
pleasant post-initiation dinner, gath
ered en masse around their pledgemaster, Emil
DiLorio, '69, shook his hand, thanked him, cheered
him, and, to a man, rushed him off to do tit for tat.
Their leader, and a
goodly number of the group
wound up in the shower duly giving him an un
necessary bath, but a symbol of how well they
had learned to stand together, share each other's
ordeals and thoughts, and to agree that what was
good for them was good for him who passed on so
well the tradition of unity among men and the
working together of Brothers for the good of each.
This is only one phase of the 130-year-old his
tory of the Delta Chapter to which so much tradi
tion has been added over the years. The hoary re
spect for these time-added processes was very
much in evidence when Doug Gerritson, '68,
called the Monday night meeting to order, ap
proved a motion to dispense with the regular order
of business, and admitted the chosen 16 to the
dimly-hghted 70-year-old Lodge Hall of the Delta.
A well organized team presented this large group
of neophytes who, in turn, clearly enunciated their
approval of being elected to Psi Upsilon and
signed the ancient Constitution as the latest en
tries on a list dating back to February 3, 1837.

by Robert R. Reinhart, Jr., '68
The following is an article which appeared in
the winter edition of The Owlet, The Epsilon
Omega's publication. With good reason it was sent
along to us by the Northwestern chapters Corre
sponding Secretary Tom Aldrich. It reflects on the
enthusiasm of a chapter as it faces a future in
which a new chapter house figures prominently.
Somehow, though, it does much more than that:
it reflects the dynamism at work in any good chap
ter, and, equally important, it says something
about attitude itself. Life is to those who live it;
not to those who sit and wait for what they think
it owes them. If a whole chapter can learn this
lesson by their association one with another then
fraternity has exhibited and fulfilled one of its
most important and valuable functions.
Robert R. Reinhart, Jr., is President of the Epsi
lon Omega Chapter.
When the Diamond Club was first conceived
back in 1947, the obstacles facing the young aspi
rant fratemity in the firmly established North
western system were many. Several, too were the
opportunities for achievement and gratification.
Far from dissipating, the basic circumstance has
sharpened over the past 20 years. Although all
the various aspects of the fraternity have under
gone great transformation over these years, the
same
impetus for growth and many problemssimilar, at least, in gravity�still confront Psi U at
Northwestem in 1968.
Moving Through Adolescence
The initiation of the largest and unquestionably
one of the best classes ever this past month indi
cated clearly the present energetic thrust of our
fraternity. The hard campaigning and personal
involvement featured in the recent chapter elec
tions also brought focus to bear both on the hard
problems still facing our evolving organization and
the prevaihng individual commitment to meet the
challenges those difficulties pose.
The Brothers are beginning to make a close ex
amination of their fraternity�one which is, after
all, still moving through adolescence in compari
son to other much older chapters. As a result of
this appraisal, answers are being sought and
found; changes demanded and realized; criticisms
made and acted upon.
Zeal for Excellence
The by-products of this rather pervasive zeal
for excellence are not consistently positive. Con
structive evaluation occasionally slides into dis
ruptive cynicism. Impatience wrought by disil
lusionment occasionally provokes apathy. But per
haps these growing pains are to be realistically,
although not complacently, expected.
The important observation to be made ( and not
unjustifiably) is that Psi U's today, here at North
westem, are predominantly excited by their house
and the dynamism they see reflected by it. They
sincerely feel they have hold of a
good thing, all
the more precious because of its inherently ephem
eral nature. They ought not be too harshly con
demned, perhaps, if they grow impatient and are
frustrated by the elusiveness of that which they
seek.
In more than one significant way, Psi U at
Northwestern is simply but very really growing up.

made up primarily of college graduates in their
early twenties. Students considering the Peace Corps
as one of several options after graduation are natu
rally interested in what it's like to be a Volunteer.
John Lane's article provides a good picture of his

one with which many returned Volun
teers would agree. This article deals with the Peace
Corps from a staff member's perspective.
I joined the Peace Corps as a Volunteer in 1963,
having just obtained a Master's degree in education,
and I was in the first group to arrive in the West
African country of Guinea. My experience as a teach
er there interested me very much in continuing in
ternational work, so upon my return to the United
States I applied for a job at Peace Corps headquar
ters, where I have worked in a variety of jobs, most
recently as an evaluator.
To most Americans the words Peace Corps bring
to mind idealistic young people working for low pay
in remote spots of the world, speaking odd lan
guages, and eating unpalatable food. While a lot
more is known today than six years ago about what
it's really like to be a Volunteer, thanks in large part
to the more than 10,000 volunteers who have com27

pleted service, most people still have a stereotype
of the Peace Corps experience�
they think it's the
same in Nigeria as in Nepal.
By way of contrast most Volunteers view the Peace
Corps and, more specifically, their particular assign
ment very clearly. Where "outsiders" see similari
ties between Peace Corps activities. Volunteers see
differences. To them the Peace Corps is an intensely
individual experience. Most Volunteers resist making
international comparisons, and even local compari
sons between the cities, where some Volunteers
work, and the smaller villages. In fact some Volun
teers become very chauvinistic about their temporary
living place. "My" country becomes no longer the
United States, but a country which most people have
never heard of.
It is interesting that, despite the differences in their
specific experiences and their unwillingness to gen
eralize, most Volunteers, especially after the com
pletion of their service, feel that they share a com
mon bond. Back in the United States where their
neighbors have, during their absence, pursued "busi
ness as usual," the Volunteers, who have stepped
outside their own culture for two years, share a
somewhat different perspective.
The Peace Corps staff is largely unknown by the
public. Staff members are generally older than most
Volunteers, receive salaries, and are responsible for
the administration of Peace Corps programs. The
overseas staff, many of whom are former Volunteers,
plan the programs with host country officials, try to
insure that good jobs exist for Volunteers before the
Volunteers arrive, and support and direct the work
of the Volunteers. Their jobs require a thorough
understanding of the host country culture as well as
an ability to provide leadership. The jobs are very
difficult. For to understand the individual problems of
many Volunteers, often in remote and trying spots,
and to handle administrative details and relations

and set a tone so that they won't be needed
with the host country government takes more time
than is available.
In addition, creating the right kind of supervision
is a job which few people can do properly. Most
Volimteers function best v^en left alone; but if left
too much alone, they may falter. The experience of
some private organizations, and of the Peace Corps
from time to time, has shown that lack of adequate
support can result in serious problems. The staff
must be there when needed, but must also plan in
advance and set a tone so that they won't be needed.
As David Berlew, Peace Corps Director in Ethiopia,
once wrote, "Most Volunteers don't like to admit it,
but the opinions of staff members are very important
to them . . .
thus, if we consistently communicate to
Volunteers our very high expectations of them, our
faith in their capacity to do the difficult and occa
sionally the impossible, they will tend to measure up
to our expectations."
In addition to the overseas staff there is a head
quarters staff which works in a 12-story office build
ing across from the White House in Washington,
D.C. To some the work seems "bureaucratic." For
example, one of 30 college students who worked at
the Peace Corps in an intern program last summer
wrote, "My advice is to close down Peace Corps
Washington, have about five people here to hand
out airline tickets and first aid kits to Volunteers and
wish them good luck." Some former Volunteers who
have gone to work for Peace Corps headquarters
have complained that they are not able to make
themselves heard in the bureaucratic atmosphere.
My experience has been that, although there is a
lot more paperwork at the Peace Corps than either
in college or overseas, life there is seldom duU. There
is constant change caused by a rapid turnover in
staff; there is the continuing challenge of dealing
with the needs of Volunteers in the most distant
parts of the world; there is the need to deal with
issues of the most difficult sort. For example, what is
a successful Volunteer? How large should a certain
program be? What is the best way to train a history
major to work in agricultural extension? How can
we measure whether our programs are accomplish
ing their objectives? And what should these objectivs be in the first place? Finally, in an organization
which operates all over the world, there are al
ways "crises," such as the Peace Corps' expulsion
from Mauritania, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli
war, with which both Washington and overseas staff
must deal.
One way of understanding why Peace Corps
Washington exists and what it does is to look in
brief and simplified fashion at the process by which
a person becomes a Volunteer, goes overseas, and
after two years, comes home. First, as a college
student, a prospective Volunteer may talk to a
former Volunteer who works for the Office of Re
cruiting. He will be asked to fill out an application,
which goes to the Office of Selection. This office in
coordination with other offices such as the medical
office and the four Regional Offices (Africa, Latin
America, East Asia and Pacific, and North Africa,
Near East and South Asia) determines whether his
qualifications are suitable for a specific request made
by a host country. As far as possible, selection hon
ors individual requests by applicants. Determining
priorities among programs and coordinating the re
quests with the available applicants is basically the
job of the Office of Planning and Program Review.
If qualified, the applicant will be placed in a
program and invited to a training program for that
country. Each Region has several training officers
whose job it is to make sure that the best training
possible is obtained for specific programs. The train
ing officer works as a kind of middle man between
the overseas staff and the universities, which do
some of Peace Corps' training and the Peace Corps'
own training centers.
Assuming the trainee successfully completes train
ing and is sent overseas (assisted by the Office of
Volunteer Support) he will find his major contact
with the overseas staff. Once or twice he may talk
with an evaluator from the Washington office and at

the end of his service he will be involved in a termi
nation conference led by a member of the Washing
ton staff. Again, his trip home and any subsequent
assistance will be provided by the Office of Volun
teer Support. The returned Volunteer may make use
of the Career Information Service, which compiles
lists of jobs in which former Volunteers might be
interested.
Other offices in Washington exist to select and
train overseas staff members, to work with Congress,
to manage the budget, and to insure that administra
tion flows smoothly.
The object of all this activity is the welfare and
success of the Volunteers. If the Peace Corps is to
continue to make a contribution to the less developed
countries, it must look ahead, and must insure that
Peace Corps programs retain the promise of 1961.
While many college students question their govern
ment, particularly because of the war in Vietnam,
it is my feeling that the Peace Corps must stand or
fall on its own. The Peace Corps is the only govern
ment program which allows people from other coun
tries to come to know Americans personally, through
the actions of individuals, regardless of the position
of the government which sends them. Volunteers
usually judge their experience on a level quite dif
ferent from that of politics and power.
In conclusion, we should not forget that there are
a great many problems in the world today which
do not get headlines. These problems will become
more acute unless people are willing to try and
solve them. Ignorance, hunger, and poverty are
more than words; they reflect conditions which de
serve attention. The Peace Corps is one way to pro
vide such attention. It is both a chance to do some
thing which matters and a chance to learn much
about the world, about the United States, and about
oneself.

century education has imposed. The word "fra
ternity" presently bears in the minds of educators

universities everywhere. We of the Kappa, conse
quently, are seeking new ways in which we might

use a contemporary cliche. We would like Psi U
to be a meaningful, relevant, and important part

longing the dining time have all met with great

ly sanctioned. The Kappa's largest adventure,

warding.

astically looking forward to having you all here.
